# unsafe-libyaml 0.2.11 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/unsafe-libyaml/latest

# unsafe-libyaml

This library is [libyaml](https://github.com/yaml/libyaml/tree/2c891fc7a770e8ba2fec34fc6b545c672beb37e6) translated from C to unsafe Rust with the assistance
of [c2rust](https://github.com/immunant/c2rust).

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
*Compiler support: requires rustc 1.56+*

## License

MIT license, same as libyaml.

---

# pretty_assertions - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pretty_assertions/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#pretty-assertions)Pretty Assertions

When writing tests in Rust, you’ll probably use `assert_eq!(a, b)` *a lot*.

If such a test fails, it will present all the details of `a` and `b`.
But you have to spot the differences yourself, which is not always straightforward,
like here:

Wouldn’t that task be *much* easier with a colorful diff?

Yep — and you only need **one line of code** to make it happen:

`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`## Show the example behind the screenshots above.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// 1. add the `pretty_assertions` dependency to `Cargo.toml`.
// 2. insert this line at the top of each module, as needed
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Foo {
    lorem: &'static str,
    ipsum: u32,
    dolor: Result<String, String>,
}
let x = Some(Foo { lorem: "Hello World!", ipsum: 42, dolor: Ok("hey".to_string())});
let y = Some(Foo { lorem: "Hello Wrold!", ipsum: 42, dolor: Ok("hey ho!".to_string())});
assert_eq!(x, y);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#tip)Tip

Specify it as [ [dev-dependencies]](http://doc.crates.io/specifying-dependencies.html#development-dependencies)
and it will only be used for compiling tests, examples, and benchmarks.
This way the compile time of

`cargo build` won’t be affected!Also add `#[cfg(test)]` to your `use` statements, like this:

```
#[cfg(test)]
use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

- Since `Rust 2018`edition, you need to declare`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`per module. Before you would write`#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions;`.
- The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries you include.
- `assert_ne`is also switched to multi-line presentation, but does- *not*show a diff.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Features provided by the crate are:

- `std`: Use the Rust standard library. Enabled by default. Exactly one of- `std`and- `alloc`is required.
- `alloc`: Use the- `alloc`crate. Exactly one of- `std`and- `alloc`is required.
- `unstable`: opt-in to unstable features that may not follow Semantic Versioning. The implementation behind this feature is subject to change without warning between patch versions.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq.html)- eq
- Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using `PartialEq`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_matches.html)- matches
- Asserts that a value matches a pattern.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_ne.html)- ne
- Asserts that two expressions are not equal to each other (using `PartialEq`
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_str_eq.html)- str_ - eq
- Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using `PartialEq`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Comparison](https://docs.rs/struct.Comparison.html)
- A comparison of two values.
- [StrComparison](https://docs.rs/struct.StrComparison.html)
- A comparison of two strings.

---

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

---

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

---

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

---

# OSX

## Installation from binaries

If you've downloaded binaries from [the Tari homepage](https://tari.com/downloads), then installing the base node is
relatively simple.

- Extract the contents of the zip archive to a convenient location (e.g. `/Users/your_name/tari_node`). Since you're reading this file, you've probably done this already.
- Give the `minotari_node`executable permission to run on your machine. Right-click on the`minotari_node`executable in Finder, select`Open`, and then click`Open`. The node will exit with an error, but this is fine; all we wanted to do is tell your Mac that it's ok to run this program.
- Run `install.sh`by double clicking on it, or entering`./install.sh`in a terminal.
- When you see the node prompt, you're good to go!

```
>> help
Available commands are:
help, version, get-chain-metadata, list-peers, reset-offline-peers, ban-peer, unban-peer, list-connections, list-headers,
check-db, calc-timing, discover-peer, get-block, search-utxo, search-kernel, search-stxo, get-mempool-stats,
get-mempool-state, whoami, get-state-info, quit, exit
```
### Prerequisites

#### Linux

```
sudo apt-get install git curl build-essential cmake clang pkg-config libssl-dev libsqlite3-dev sqlite3
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
```
### From source

```
cargo install minotari_node
```

# suno_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/suno-core/0.16.1/suno_core/

## Expand description

Core engine for rs-suno: library selection, sync reconciliation, and tagging.

Runtime-agnostic and free of direct IO. Network access happens through the
[ Http](https://docs.rs/trait.Http.html) port, which a CLI adapter implements, so the engine stays testable
in isolation.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- Configuration model and precedence resolution.
- [reconcile](https://docs.rs/reconcile/index.html)
- The pure reconcile engine: it decides what to download, retag, rename, reformat, and delete.
- [select](https://docs.rs/select/index.html)
- Pure clip selection and filtering.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Album](https://docs.rs/struct.AlbumArt.html)- Art
- The reconciled folder-art state for one album (one stable root id).
- [Artifact](https://docs.rs/struct.ArtifactState.html)- State
- The prior known state of one external sidecar artifact for a clip.
- [Cache](https://docs.rs/struct.CacheEntry.html)- Entry
- A cached root resolution for one clip: the O(1) album lookup, kept monotonic.
- [Clerk](https://docs.rs/struct.ClerkAuth.html)- Auth
- Manages the Clerk cookie and the JWT lifecycle for one account.
- [Clip](https://docs.rs/struct.Clip.html)
- One finished Suno track, flattened from the API’s nested response shape.
- [Edge](https://docs.rs/struct.Edge.html)
- One parent link of a clip, for the later lineage graph store.
- [Exec](https://docs.rs/struct.ExecOptions.html)- Options
- Tunables for one `execute`
- [Exec](https://docs.rs/struct.ExecOutcome.html)- Outcome
- The result of applying a `Plan`
- [Failure](https://docs.rs/struct.Failure.html)
- One action that could not be applied, for the run summary and failure log.
- [Ffmpeg](https://docs.rs/struct.FfmpegError.html)- Error
- An ffmpeg transcode failure, carrying a kind and a human-readable, secret-free reason.
- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.FileStat.html)- Stat
- On-disk facts about one path, as probed by `Filesystem::metadata`
- [FsError](https://docs.rs/struct.FsError.html)
- A filesystem failure, carrying a kind and a human-readable, secret-free reason.
- [History](https://docs.rs/struct.HistoryEntry.html)- Entry
- One entry in a clip’s `history`or`concat_history`, mirroring the API’s per-segment lineage record. Ids are stored verbatim (any`m_`prefix is left for the resolver to strip).
- [Http](https://docs.rs/struct.HttpRequest.html)- Request
- A request the engine wants an adapter to perform.
- [Http](https://docs.rs/struct.HttpResponse.html)- Response
- The response an adapter returns to the engine.
- [Lineage](https://docs.rs/struct.LineageContext.html)- Context
- The resolved lineage of a single clip, threaded into naming, tagging, and change detection.
- [Lineage](https://docs.rs/struct.LineageStore.html)- Store
- The whole lineage graph, kept relational for a clean SQLite migration.
- [M3u8](https://docs.rs/struct.M3u8Entry.html)- Entry
- One ordered entry in an extended-M3U8 playlist.
- [Manifest](https://docs.rs/struct.Manifest.html)
- The full prior download state, keyed by clip id.
- [Manifest](https://docs.rs/struct.ManifestEntry.html)- Entry
- One manifest record: the prior known state of a single downloaded clip.
- [Naming](https://docs.rs/struct.NamingConfig.html)- Config
- [Naming](https://docs.rs/struct.NamingRequest.html)- Request
- [Node](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html)
- One clip in the graph. Mirrors the fields lineage needs to survive a purge: enough to name and date the clip long after Suno deletes it.
- [Owner](https://docs.rs/struct.Owner.html)
- The Suno account a library belongs to, pinned on first use.
- [Playlist](https://docs.rs/struct.Playlist.html)
- One of the account’s own playlists, as listed by `/api/playlist/me`.
- [Playlist](https://docs.rs/struct.PlaylistState.html)- State
- The reconciled `.m3u8`state for one playlist.
- [Ports](https://docs.rs/struct.Ports.html)
- The IO ports the executor drives, grouped so one value threads them through.
- [Rendered](https://docs.rs/struct.RenderedName.html)- Name
- [Resolution](https://docs.rs/struct.Resolution.html)
- The outcome of `resolve_roots`
- [Resolve](https://docs.rs/struct.ResolveOpts.html)- Opts
- Tunables bounding how hard `resolve_roots`
- [Root](https://docs.rs/struct.RootInfo.html)- Info
- The resolved root ancestor of a clip.
- [Stored](https://docs.rs/struct.StoredEdge.html)- Edge
- One parent link, keyed (for upsert) by `(child_id, parent_id, edge_type, role, ordinal)`. A flat row, not nested under its child, so it maps directly to a`lineage_edges`table.
- [Suno](https://docs.rs/struct.SunoClient.html)- Client
- A client for the Suno library API, owning the account’s `ClerkAuth`

- A failure to complete a request at the transport level.

# posthog_rs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/posthog-rs/0.17.2/posthog_rs/

## Expand description

Official Rust SDK for PostHog.

Use [ client](https://docs.rs/fn.client.html) to construct a

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html)

`Client`[to capture analytics events, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)

`Event`[with](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html#method.evaluate_flags)

`Client::evaluate_flags`[for feature flag evaluation.](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluateFlagsOptions.html)

`EvaluateFlagsOptions`See the [PostHog Rust SDK documentation](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/rust)
for installation, configuration, and more examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Add `posthog-rs` to your `Cargo.toml`, then initialize a client with your
project API key.

```
use posthog_rs::{client, EvaluateFlagsOptions, Event};
#[cfg(feature = "async-client")]
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), posthog_rs::Error> {
    let api_key = std::env::var("POSTHOG_API_KEY")
        .expect("set POSTHOG_API_KEY to your PostHog project API key");
    let posthog = client(api_key.as_str()).await;
    let distinct_id = "user-123";
    // Capture an analytics event.
    let mut event = Event::new("signed_up", distinct_id);
    event.insert_prop("plan", "pro")?;
    posthog.capture(event);
    // Evaluate feature flags once, then read from the snapshot.
    let flags = posthog
        .evaluate_flags(distinct_id, EvaluateFlagsOptions::default())
        .await?;
    if flags.is_enabled("new-onboarding") {
        let mut event = Event::new("onboarding_step_completed", distinct_id);
        event.with_flags(&flags.only_accessed());
        posthog.capture(event);
    }
    Ok(())
}
#[cfg(not(feature = "async-client"))]
fn main() -> Result<(), posthog_rs::Error> {
    let api_key = std::env::var("POSTHOG_API_KEY")
        .expect("set POSTHOG_API_KEY to your PostHog project API key");
    let posthog = client(api_key.as_str());
    let distinct_id = "user-123";
    // Capture an analytics event.
    let mut event = Event::new("signed_up", distinct_id);
    event.insert_prop("plan", "pro")?;
    posthog.capture(event);
    // Evaluate feature flags once, then read from the snapshot.
    let flags = posthog.evaluate_flags(distinct_id, EvaluateFlagsOptions::default())?;
    if flags.is_enabled("new-onboarding") {
        let mut event = Event::new("onboarding_step_completed", distinct_id);
        event.with_flags(&flags.only_accessed());
        posthog.capture(event);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncFlagPoller.html)- Flag - Poller
- Asynchronous poller for feature flag definitions.
- [Before](https://docs.rs/struct.BeforeSendHook.html)- Send - Hook
- Hook that can modify or discard events before they are sent.
- [Capture](https://docs.rs/struct.CaptureExceptionOptions.html)- Exception - Options
- Optional context for `capture_exception_with`: person identity, custom properties, groups, and exception fingerprint/level.
- [Capture](https://docs.rs/struct.CaptureFailure.html)- Failure
- Details of a terminal capture batch failure.
- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html)
- A `Client`
- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.ClientOptions.html)- Options
- Configuration options for the PostHog client.
- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.ClientOptionsBuilder.html)- Options - Builder
- Builder for `ClientOptions`
- [Cohort](https://docs.rs/struct.Cohort.html)

# sutegi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sutegi/0.5.1/sutegi/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#sutegi--the-forge)sutegi — the forge

A zero-dependency, agent-native web framework for Rust, built on `std`: the
HTTP/1.1 server, JSON codec, and router are always present. Everything else
is an opt-in **compile-time feature**, so you ship only what you use:

| Feature | Pulls in | Gives you |
|---|---|---|
| `orm` | sutegi-orm | schema + query builder + migrations + JSON/vector columns + embeddings + KV |
| `sqlite` | + bundled rusqlite | SQLite: the single-node execution layer |
| `postgres` | sutegi-pg (pure std) | Postgres: the multi-pod execution layer |
| `derive` | sutegi-macros (build-time only) | `#[derive(Model)]` |
| `validate` | sutegi-validate | request / tool validation |
| `ai` | sutegi-ai | `Tool`/`StreamTool`+`/__tools` |
| `queue` | sutegi-queue (+ sutegi-pg) | durable, cross-pod job queue (Postgres) |
| `session` | sutegi-session | signed-cookie sessions (HMAC-SHA256) |
| `auth` | sutegi-auth (+ session/orm) | the user system: passwords, Users, guards, API tokens |
| `template` | sutegi-template | Blade-style template engine ( `{{ }}`,`@if`,`@foreach`,`@include`) |
| `mail` | sutegi-mail (+ template) | Email builder, themed messages, Transport seam, smtp/sendmail/log drivers |
| `auth-mail` | + sutegi-auth/mail | email-verification + password-reset flows |
| `storage` | sutegi-storage (pure std) | file storage: local fs + S3 presigned URLs |
| `storage-db` | + sutegi-orm | blobs in SQLite/Postgres over the `Backend`seam |
| `graceful` | libc | SIGTERM/SIGINT draining for pods |

`default = ["derive", "orm", "validate", "ai"]`. For a minimal
HTTP service: `sutegi = { version = "*", default-features = false }`.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-operational-endpoints-always-on)Built-in operational endpoints (always on)

`GET /__health` (liveness), `GET /__ready` (readiness probe),
`GET /__metrics` (Prometheus), `GET /__introspect` (full app surface).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# sovereign_profile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sovereign-profile/0.1.2/sovereign_profile/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#8-dimensional-sovereign-profile)8-Dimensional Sovereign Profile

Anti-tyranny civic identity for the Mycelix governance system.

When you reduce a human being to a single number — like a credit score or social credit rating — you create a system that is infinitely gamifiable and inherently oppressive. The 8D Sovereign Profile maps identity as a holographic, multi-faceted geometry rather than a flat number.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-8-axes-of-civic-identity)The 8 Axes of Civic Identity

- **Epistemic Integrity**— truth/claim verification history
- **Thermodynamic Yield**— physical energy contribution to local commons
- **Network Resilience**— node uptime and bandwidth provision
- **Economic Velocity**— compliance with anti-hoarding demurrage
- **Civic Participation**— sortition jury duty, voting, dispute resolution
- **Stewardship & Care**— verified physical labor on the commons
- **Semantic Resonance**— entanglement with community consensus
- **Domain Competence**— peer-verified specialization

Each dimension is directly measurable from a primary source (smart meter, node log, transaction ledger, jury record, telemetry shim). Multiple pathways to citizenship are respected — a reclusive solar engineer and a social mediator both pass the threshold through completely different dimensional profiles.

[§](https://docs.rs#privacy)Privacy

The profile never leaves the local device. ZKP circuits prove the
*aggregate* weight exceeds a threshold without revealing individual
dimensions. The network knows you are a net-positive citizen but has
no idea *how* you achieved that.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [collectors](https://docs.rs/collectors/index.html)

- [compat](https://docs.rs/compat/index.html)
- Backward compatibility with the legacy 4D ConsciousnessProfile.
- [decay](https://docs.rs/decay/index.html)
- Parameterized exponential decay for the 8D Sovereign Profile.
- [i18n](https://docs.rs/i18n/index.html)
- Internationalization keys and labels for the 8D Sovereign Profile.
- [weights](https://docs.rs/weights/index.html)
- Community-configurable dimension weights for the 8D Sovereign Profile.

# sutegi_auth - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sutegi-auth/0.5.1/sutegi_auth/

## Expand description

The sutegi **user system** — registration, login, guards, and API tokens,
with zero third-party dependencies. The Laravel `auth` scaffolding, over
sutegi’s own seams:

- `password`
- `Users`- `Backend`: SQLite single-node or Postgres multi-pod, same calls. Hashes never leave the store.
- `Auth`- `sutegi-session`) with a- **server-side expiry**stamped into the signed payload, so a stolen cookie dies on schedule regardless of what the client claims.
- `Tokens`- **agents and services**; the plaintext is returned once and only its SHA-256 is stored.
- Route guards: `require_auth``require_role``require_token``App::group(prefix, vec![mw(...)], …)`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let db = Db::open("app.db")?;
let auth = Arc::new(Auth::new(
    Users::new(db.clone()),
    Sessions::new(config.require("SESSION_SECRET")?.as_bytes()),
));
auth.users.migrate()?;
App::new("app")
    .post("/login", "Log in.", move |c| {
        let (email, pw) = …;
        match auth.users.authenticate(&email, &pw)? {
            Some(user) => Ok(auth.login(c.req, &user, json(200, &user.to_json()))),
            None => Err(Error::unauthorized("bad credentials")),
        }
    })
    .group("/admin", vec![mw(require_role(auth.clone(), "admin"))], |g| …)
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use flows::`- [AuthMail](https://docs.rs/flows/struct.AuthMail.html);
- `pub use links::`- [Links](https://docs.rs/links/struct.Links.html);
- `pub use password::`- [hash_password](https://docs.rs/password/fn.hash_password.html);
- `pub use password::`- [verify_password](https://docs.rs/password/fn.verify_password.html);
- `pub use password::`- [DEFAULT_ITERATIONS](https://docs.rs/password/constant.DEFAULT_ITERATIONS.html);
- `pub use tokens::`- [ApiToken](https://docs.rs/tokens/struct.ApiToken.html);
- `pub use tokens::`- [Tokens](https://docs.rs/tokens/struct.Tokens.html);
- `pub use tokens::`- [TOKEN_PREFIX](https://docs.rs/tokens/constant.TOKEN_PREFIX.html);
- `pub use users::`- [User](https://docs.rs/users/struct.User.html);
- `pub use users::`- [Users](https://docs.rs/users/struct.Users.html);
- `pub use users::`- [MIN_PASSWORD_LEN](https://docs.rs/users/constant.MIN_PASSWORD_LEN.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [flows](https://docs.rs/flows/index.html)
- The auth mail flows (feature `mail`):**email verification**and**password reset**, Laravel-defaults style — sensible templates, signed expiring links, no state tables.
- [links](https://docs.rs/links/index.html)
- Expiring, purpose-scoped **signed tokens**for email links (verification, password reset). Stateless:`purpose | uid | exp | bind`is hex-encoded and HMAC-SHA256-signed; nothing is stored. The`bind`slot ties a token to a piece of current state (e.g. a fingerprint of the password hash) so the token dies when that state changes.
- [password](https://docs.rs/password/index.html)
- Password hashing: **PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256**with a per-password random salt, serialized as a PHC-style string:
- [tokens](https://docs.rs/tokens/index.html)
- API tokens — how **agents and services**authenticate, where cookie sessions don’t fit. The Sanctum-shaped deal:
- [users](https://docs.rs/users/index.html)
- The `Users`store: registration, credential checks, and lookups over any ORM`Backend`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Auth](https://docs.rs/struct.Auth.html)
- The session glue: a `Users``Sessions`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [require_](https://docs.rs/fn.require_auth.html)- auth
- Guard: reject with `401`JSON unless the request carries a valid session. Cookie-signature work only — handlers needing the full user call`Auth::current`
- [require_](https://docs.rs/fn.require_role.html)- role
- Guard: `401`without a valid session,`403`unless the logged-in user carries`role`(one store lookup per request).
- [require_](https://docs.rs/fn.require_token.html)- token
- Guard: reject with `401`unless the request carries a valid`Authorization: Bearer stg_…`API token — the agent/service door. Handlers can identify the caller with`token_user`
- [token_](https://docs.rs/fn.token_user.html)- user
- Resolve the request’s bearer token to its owning `User``require_token`

# sutegi_session - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sutegi-session/0.5.1/sutegi_session/

## Expand description

Signed-cookie sessions for sutegi.

State lives in an HMAC-SHA256-signed cookie — stateless on the server, and
tamper-evident (a modified payload fails verification and is discarded).
Signing uses [ sutegi_crypto](https://docs.rs/sutegi-crypto/0.5.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sutegi_crypto/index.html)’s known-answer-tested HMAC-SHA256 (the same
implementation the Postgres driver’s SCRAM auth rides), so this crate has

**zero third-party dependencies**.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let sessions = Sessions::new(b"a-32+ byte secret from your config");
// in a handler:
let mut s = sessions.load(req);
s.set("user_id", Json::int(42));
sessions.save(&s, json(200, &Json::obj(vec![("ok", Json::Bool(true))])))
```

---

# sutegi_hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sutegi-hex/0.5.1/sutegi_hex/

## Expand description

Opinionated building blocks for **hexagonal / clean architecture** in sutegi.

The shape this crate nudges you toward:

```
           inbound adapters                     outbound adapters
        (HTTP handlers, AI tools)            (SQLite repo, HTTP client)
                   │  call                          ▲  implement
                   ▼                                │
           ┌───────────────┐   depends on    ┌──────────────┐
           │  application  │ ───────────────▶│    ports     │
           │  (use cases)  │                 │   (traits)   │
           └───────┬───────┘                 └──────────────┘
                   │ uses
                   ▼
           ┌───────────────┐
           │    domain     │  (pure: entities + rules, no framework)
           └───────────────┘
```
**The dependency rule:** source dependencies point *inward*. Domain knows
nothing of the application; the application knows ports but not their
concrete adapters; adapters depend on the application/ports — never the
reverse. sutegi’s HTTP and AI layers are just *inbound adapters*; a database
is just an *outbound adapter*. Swap either without touching the core.

This crate gives you the three things that make that ergonomic:

- `AppError`
- `UseCase`
- `respond`- `respond_created`- `AppResult<T>`to a- `Response`, so inbound HTTP adapters are one line.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.EventBus.html)- Bus
- A type-keyed event bus. Register handlers with `EventBus::on``EventBus::dispatch`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [AppError](https://docs.rs/enum.AppError.html)
- A transport-agnostic application/domain error. Lives in the inner layers; adapters map it to their transport (the HTTP mapping is provided here as the house convention).

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Command](https://docs.rs/trait.Command.html)
- A **command**— a write intent. Consumes itself (one-shot) and returns its result. The write side of CQRS; pair with`Query`
- [Event](https://docs.rs/trait.Event.html)
- A domain **event**— something that happened. Dispatch via an`EventBus`
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoJson.html)- Json
- Presentation: how an outbound value becomes JSON at the adapter boundary.
Implement this in the *adapter*layer for your domain types so the domain itself stays free of transport concerns.
- [Query](https://docs.rs/trait.Query.html)
- A **query**— a read intent. Borrows itself (idempotent, repeatable) and returns data. The read side of CQRS.
- [Repository](https://docs.rs/trait.Repository.html)
- An optional generic **outbound-port**convention for persistence. Real ports are usually domain-specific (e.g.`TodoRepository`); this is here for the simple CRUD case. Define your own trait when the domain needs richer queries.
- [UseCase](https://docs.rs/trait.UseCase.html)
- An **inbound port**: a single application use case. Input and Output are plain domain/DTO types — the use case never sees HTTP or JSON, which is what keeps the core testable and transport-independent.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [respond](https://docs.rs/fn.respond.html)
- Adapter glue: map an `AppResult<T>`to a`200`response (or the error’s canonical response). This is what makes an inbound HTTP adapter a one-liner.
- [respond_](https://docs.rs/fn.respond_created.html)- created
- Like `respond``201 Created`on success.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [AppResult](https://docs.rs/type.AppResult.html)
- The result type used throughout the application and domain layers.

---

# sutegi_storage - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sutegi-storage/0.5.1/sutegi_storage/

## Expand description

File/object storage behind one trait — the storage counterpart to the ORM’s
`Backend` seam: **swap the backend, not the call sites.**

- `FsStorage`- **single-node default**: zero-ops, zero deps, real streaming reads. The SQLite of file storage.
- `DbStorage`- `db`) — blobs in a database table over any ORM- `Backend`. On Postgres this is- **multi-pod file storage with zero new infrastructure**— the database you already run is the blob store. Good to roughly a few MB per object; past that, reach for real object storage.
- `S3Store`- `std`- **SigV4 presigner**for S3-compatible object stores (AWS, R2, MinIO, …). It mints time-limited GET/PUT/DELETE URLs; the bytes flow- **directly between the client (or agent) and S3**, never through sutegi. That is why it needs no HTTP client and no TLS — signing is HMAC-SHA256, reused from the Postgres driver’s SCRAM implementation.

`S3Store` deliberately does **not** implement [ Storage](https://docs.rs/trait.Storage.html): handing out a
URL is a different contract than moving bytes. When a full S3 client lands
(blocked on TLS), it will join the trait; until then the swap seam spans
fs ↔ db, and S3 is the presign-only escape hatch.

Keys are `/`-separated paths (`avatars/42.png`), validated identically
across backends — see [ validate_key](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_key.html).

```
use sutegi_storage::{FsStorage, Storage};
let store = FsStorage::new("data/files").unwrap();
store.put("hello.txt", b"hi", "text/plain").unwrap();
let bytes = store.get("hello.txt").unwrap(); // Some(vec![...])
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [db](https://docs.rs/db/index.html)
- Blobs in a database table, over any ORM `Backend`
- [fs](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html)
- Local-filesystem storage — the **single-node default**. One directory on disk, keys map to relative paths, writes are atomic (temp file + rename).
- [s3](https://docs.rs/s3/index.html)
- A pure-`std`**AWS Signature V4 presigner**for S3-compatible object stores. It mints time-limited GET/PUT/DELETE URLs; the bytes then flow directly between the holder of the URL (a browser, a`curl`, an agent) and the object store —**sutegi never proxies them**.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Object](https://docs.rs/struct.ObjectMeta.html)- Meta
- What a backend knows about a stored object.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Storage](https://docs.rs/trait.Storage.html)
- A byte-level object store. Implemented by `FsStorage``DbStorage``impl Storage`(or a concrete type) and swaps backends by changing the type it constructs, not the call sites.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [content_](https://docs.rs/fn.content_type_of.html)- type_ - of
- A best-effort MIME type from a key’s extension;
`application/octet-stream`when unknown.
- [validate_](https://docs.rs/fn.validate_key.html)- key
- Validate an object key. Enforced identically by every backend so a key
valid on one is valid on all: non-empty, at most 1024 bytes, `/`-separated non-empty segments, no`.`/`..`segments (path traversal), no backslashes or control characters, and no segment starting with`.sutegi-`(reserved for backend internals such as`FsStorage`

# sutegi_ai - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sutegi-ai/0.5.1/sutegi_ai/

## Expand description

Agent-facing surface for sutegi.

Tools are now a **core** concept: register them directly on the app with
[ App::tool](https://docs.rs/sutegi-web/0.5.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sutegi_web/struct.App.html#method.tool) / [

`App::stream_tool`], and describe
their inputs with the [helpers. sutegi validates each call’s arguments against the declared schema, mounts](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)

`schema``POST /__tools/:name`
(and `/__tools/:name/stream` for SSE), and lists everything in the
`/__tools` manifest and `/__introspect`.[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use sutegi::prelude::*;
App::new("assistant")
    .state(db)
    .tool("create_todo", "Create a todo",
        schema::object(vec![("title", schema::string("the title"))], &["title"]),
        |c, args| {
            let todo: Todo = Todo::from_row(&args)?;   // args are validated
            let id = todo.save(c.db::<Db>())?;
            Ok(Todo { id, ..todo }.to_json())
        })
    .serve()
```
This crate re-exports that surface so the `sutegi::ai::…` path keeps working
and is the home for future LLM-client helpers.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Helpers to construct JSON Schema fragments for tool `parameters`, so declaring a tool’s inputs reads declaratively instead of as nested map building. Used with`App::tool`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ctx](https://docs.rs/struct.Ctx.html)
- Everything a request handler needs: the `Request``Params`
- [ToolCtx](https://docs.rs/struct.ToolCtx.html)
- The owned context handed to AI tool closures (`App::tool``App::stream_tool``Ctx`

# sutegi_web - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sutegi-web/0.5.1/sutegi_web/

## Expand description

The web spine: a route table, middleware chain, ergonomic extractors, and
the runtime **introspection registry** that makes a sutegi app
self-describing.

Every route is registered with a human/agent-readable doc string. Models
and tools register their schemas. At runtime, `GET /__introspect` returns
the full surface of the application as JSON — so an AI agent can discover
what the app can do without ever reading the source.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)
- Helpers to construct JSON Schema fragments for tool `parameters`, so declaring a tool’s inputs reads declaratively instead of as nested map building. Used with`App::tool`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [App](https://docs.rs/struct.App.html)
- The application: a builder you configure with routes, state, tools, and
middleware, then `serve()`(or`run()`).
- [Ctx](https://docs.rs/struct.Ctx.html)
- Everything a request handler needs: the `Request``Params`
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- A transport-agnostic error that converts into an HTTP `Response`
- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A builder for a group of routes sharing a prefix and middleware. Created via
`App::group`
- [Limits](https://docs.rs/struct.Limits.html)
- Server resource limits — the difference between “demo” and “won’t fall over”.
- [Request](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html)
- A parsed HTTP request.
- [Response](https://docs.rs/struct.Response.html)
- An HTTP response.
- [SseSink](https://docs.rs/struct.SseSink.html)
- A flushing sink that formats Server-Sent Events (`text/event-stream`). Each call emits one event frame and flushes — exactly what LLM token streaming wants.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamSink.html)- Sink
- A flushing sink for raw streamed bytes. Every `write`is flushed so the client sees data immediately.
- [ToolCtx](https://docs.rs/struct.ToolCtx.html)
- The owned context handed to AI tool closures (`App::tool``App::stream_tool``Ctx`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoResponse.html)- Response
- Anything a handler may return. Converts into a concrete `Response`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [basic](https://docs.rs/fn.basic.html)
- A pre-middleware requiring HTTP Basic auth for `user`/`pass`; else`401`.
- [bearer](https://docs.rs/fn.bearer.html)
- A pre-middleware requiring `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; else`401`.
- [cors](https://docs.rs/fn.cors.html)
- An after-middleware that stamps `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`onto every response. Register with`App::after`
- [cors_](https://docs.rs/fn.cors_preflight.html)- preflight
- A pre-middleware that answers CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) with`204`and the permitted origin. Pair with`cors`
- [form_](https://docs.rs/fn.form_body.html)- body
- Parse an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`request body into a map.
- [html](https://docs.rs/fn.html.html)
- A `text/html`response.
- [json](https://docs.rs/fn.json.html)
- An `application/json`response from a`Json`value.
- [json_](https://docs.rs/fn.json_body.html)- body
- Parse the request body as JSON.
- [logger](https://docs.rs/fn.logger.html)
- A pre-middleware that logs `METHOD /path`for each request and continues.
- [mw](https://docs.rs/fn.mw.html)
- Wrap a closure as a shareable group middleware.
- [no_](https://docs.rs/fn.no_content.html)- content
- A `204 No Content`.
- [not_](https://docs.rs/fn.not_found.html)- found
- A canned 404.
- [query_](https://docs.rs/fn.query_params.html)- params
- Parse the query string into a map (`a=1&b=2`→`{a:1, b:2}`).
- [rate_](https://docs.rs/fn.rate_limit.html)- limit
- A per-client-IP token-bucket rate limiter (pre-middleware). Allows bursts up
to `max_requests`, refilling over`per`; returns`429`when exhausted.
- [redirect](https://docs.rs/fn.redirect.html)
- A `302 Found`redirect to`location`.
- [secure_](https://docs.rs/fn.secure_headers.html)- headers
- An after-middleware adding a baseline set of security headers (nosniff,
frame-deny, referrer-policy, HSTS). Register with `App::after`
- [sse](https://docs.rs/fn.sse.html)
- A Server-Sent Events response. `producer`pushes events through an`SseSink``data`/`event`/`comment`), each flushed immediately — the natural transport for streaming LLM tokens to a browser or agent.
- [status](https://docs.rs/fn.status.html)
- An empty response with just a status code.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/fn.stream.html)
- A streaming response: `producer`writes (and flushes) bytes over time via a`StreamSink``content_type`; no`Content-Length`.
- [text](https://docs.rs/fn.text.html)
- A `text/plain`response.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [After](https://docs.rs/type.AfterMiddleware.html)- Middleware
- An after-middleware: transforms the outgoing response (e.g. adds headers).
- [Handler](https://docs.rs/type.Handler.html)
- A request handler: takes a `Ctx``Response``IntoResponse`
- [Middleware](https://docs.rs/type.Middleware.html)
- A middleware: inspects a request before routing. Returning `Some(resp)`short-circuits (e.g. auth rejection);`None`lets the request continue.
- [Mw](https://docs.rs/type.Mw.html)
- A reference-counted, shareable middleware (build with `mw`
- [MwFn](https://docs.rs/type.MwFn.html)
- The shareable form of a middleware, used by route groups.
- [Params](https://docs.rs/type.Params.html)
- Path parameters captured from a route pattern (`:name`segments).

# sutegi_queue - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sutegi-queue/0.5.1/sutegi_queue/

## Expand description

A **durable, cross-pod** job queue backed by PostgreSQL — built to survive
restarts and span replicas.

Jobs live in a `sutegi_jobs` table. Any number of app pods can enqueue and
process from the same queue: workers claim a job atomically with
`SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so two workers never grab the same row.
A claim sets a lock timestamp rather than deleting the row, so if a worker
crashes mid-job the row becomes visible again after a visibility timeout —
giving **at-least-once** delivery. Retries and delayed dispatch are columns,
not in-memory timers, so they survive restarts.

Jobs are addressed by **name**: you register a handler per job name, and the
payload travels as JSON. That’s what lets a job enqueued on one pod run on
another. Build the queue over a [ sutegi_pg::Pool](https://docs.rs/sutegi-pg/0.5.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sutegi_pg/pool/struct.Pool.html):

```
use std::sync::Arc;
use sutegi_queue::Queue;
use sutegi_json::Json;
let mut queue = Queue::new(pool);
queue.register("send_email", |payload: &Json| {
    // … do the work, return Err to retry …
    Ok(())
});
queue.migrate()?;
queue.dispatch("send_email", Json::obj(vec![("to", Json::str("a@b.c"))]))?;
let queue = Arc::new(queue);
let _workers = Arc::clone(&queue).start(4); // background workers until dropped
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Queue](https://docs.rs/struct.Queue.html)
- A durable queue over a PostgreSQL connection pool.
- [Workers](https://docs.rs/struct.Workers.html)
- A running set of queue workers. Dropping it (or calling [`stop`] (Workers::stop)) signals shutdown and joins the threads.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Handler](https://docs.rs/type.Handler.html)
- A handler for a named job: receives the decoded JSON payload. Returning
`Err`triggers a retry (until the job’s attempt budget is exhausted).

## Fields (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

## This struct is marked as non-exhaustive

Non-exhaustive structs could have additional fields added in future. Therefore, non-exhaustive structs cannot be constructed in external crates using the traditional

`Struct { .. }` syntax; cannot be matched against without a wildcard `..`; and struct update syntax will not work.[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.type_)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.data)

`data: unnamed_yaml_event_t_data`The event data.

```
union {
    /// The stream parameters (for YAML_STREAM_START_EVENT).
    stream_start: struct {
        /// The document encoding.
        encoding: yaml_encoding_t,
    },
    /// The document parameters (for YAML_DOCUMENT_START_EVENT).
    document_start: struct {
        /// The version directive.
        version_directive: *mut yaml_version_directive_t,
        /// The list of tag directives.
        tag_directives: struct {
            /// The beginning of the tag directives list.
            start: *mut yaml_tag_directive_t,
            /// The end of the tag directives list.
            end: *mut yaml_tag_directive_t,
        },
        /// Is the document indicator implicit?
        implicit: i32,
    },
    /// The document end parameters (for YAML_DOCUMENT_END_EVENT).
    document_end: struct {
        /// Is the document end indicator implicit?
        implicit: i32,
    },
    /// The alias parameters (for YAML_ALIAS_EVENT).
    alias: struct {
        /// The anchor.
        anchor: *mut u8,
    },
    /// The scalar parameters (for YAML_SCALAR_EVENT).
    scalar: struct {
        /// The anchor.
        anchor: *mut u8,
        /// The tag.
        tag: *mut u8,
        /// The scalar value.
        value: *mut u8,
        /// The length of the scalar value.
        length: u64,
        /// Is the tag optional for the plain style?
        plain_implicit: i32,
        /// Is the tag optional for any non-plain style?
        quoted_implicit: i32,
        /// The scalar style.
        style: yaml_scalar_style_t,
    },
    /// The sequence parameters (for YAML_SEQUENCE_START_EVENT).
    sequence_start: struct {
        /// The anchor.
        anchor: *mut u8,
        /// The tag.
        tag: *mut u8,
        /// Is the tag optional?
        implicit: i32,
        /// The sequence style.
        style: yaml_sequence_style_t,
    },
    /// The mapping parameters (for YAML_MAPPING_START_EVENT).
    mapping_start: struct {
        /// The anchor.
        anchor: *mut u8,
        /// The tag.
        tag: *mut u8,
        /// Is the tag optional?
        implicit: i32,
        /// The mapping style.
        style: yaml_mapping_style_t,
    },
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.start_mark)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.end_mark)

# yaml_break_t in unsafe_libyaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unsafe-libyaml/0.2.11/unsafe_libyaml/enum.yaml_break_t.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]#[repr(u32)]pub enum yaml_break_t {
    YAML_ANY_BREAK = 0,
    YAML_CR_BREAK = 1,
    YAML_LN_BREAK = 2,
    YAML_CRLN_BREAK = 3,
}
```
## Expand description

Line break type.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

Non-exhaustive enums could have additional variants added in future. Therefore, when matching against variants of non-exhaustive enums, an extra wildcard arm must be added to account for any future variants.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_ANY_BREAK)

### YAML_ANY_BREAK = 0

Let the parser choose the break type.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_CR_BREAK)

### YAML_CR_BREAK = 1

Use CR for line breaks (Mac style).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_LN_BREAK)

### YAML_LN_BREAK = 2

Use LN for line breaks (Unix style).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_CRLN_BREAK)

### YAML_CRLN_BREAK = 3

Use CR LN for line breaks (DOS style).

# yaml_error_type_t in unsafe_libyaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unsafe-libyaml/0.2.11/unsafe_libyaml/enum.yaml_error_type_t.html

```
#[non_exhaustive]#[repr(u32)]pub enum yaml_error_type_t {
    YAML_NO_ERROR = 0,
    YAML_MEMORY_ERROR = 1,
    YAML_READER_ERROR = 2,
    YAML_SCANNER_ERROR = 3,
    YAML_PARSER_ERROR = 4,
    YAML_COMPOSER_ERROR = 5,
    YAML_WRITER_ERROR = 6,
    YAML_EMITTER_ERROR = 7,
}
```
## Expand description

Many bad things could happen with the parser and emitter.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_NO_ERROR)

### YAML_NO_ERROR = 0

No error is produced.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_MEMORY_ERROR)

### YAML_MEMORY_ERROR = 1

Cannot allocate or reallocate a block of memory.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_READER_ERROR)

### YAML_READER_ERROR = 2

Cannot read or decode the input stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_SCANNER_ERROR)

### YAML_SCANNER_ERROR = 3

Cannot scan the input stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_PARSER_ERROR)

### YAML_PARSER_ERROR = 4

Cannot parse the input stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_COMPOSER_ERROR)

### YAML_COMPOSER_ERROR = 5

Cannot compose a YAML document.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_WRITER_ERROR)

### YAML_WRITER_ERROR = 6

Cannot write to the output stream.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_EMITTER_ERROR)

### YAML_EMITTER_ERROR = 7

Cannot emit a YAML stream.

## Expand description

Sequence styles.

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

Non-exhaustive enums could have additional variants added in future. Therefore, when matching against variants of non-exhaustive enums, an extra wildcard arm must be added to account for any future variants.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_ANY_SEQUENCE_STYLE)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YAML_FLOW_SEQUENCE_STYLE)

# yaml_parser_load in unsafe_libyaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unsafe-libyaml/0.2.11/unsafe_libyaml/fn.yaml_parser_load.html

```
pub unsafe fn yaml_parser_load(
    parser:
```
[*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html)[yaml_parser_t](https://docs.rs/struct.yaml_parser_t.html),
    document: [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html)[yaml_document_t](https://docs.rs/struct.yaml_document_t.html),
) -> Success## Expand description

Parse the input stream and produce the next YAML document.

Call this function subsequently to produce a sequence of documents constituting the input stream.

If the produced document has no root node, it means that the document end has been reached.

An application is responsible for freeing any data associated with the produced document object using the yaml_document_delete() function.

An application must not alternate the calls of yaml_parser_load() with the calls of yaml_parser_scan() or yaml_parser_parse(). Doing this will break the parser.

---

# yaml_parser_parse in unsafe_libyaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unsafe-libyaml/0.2.11/unsafe_libyaml/fn.yaml_parser_parse.html

```
pub unsafe fn yaml_parser_parse(
    parser:
```
[*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html)[yaml_parser_t](https://docs.rs/struct.yaml_parser_t.html),
    event: [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html)[yaml_event_t](https://docs.rs/struct.yaml_event_t.html),
) -> Success## Expand description

Parse the input stream and produce the next parsing event.

Call the function subsequently to produce a sequence of events corresponding to the input stream. The initial event has the type YAML_STREAM_START_EVENT while the ending event has the type YAML_STREAM_END_EVENT.

An application is responsible for freeing any buffers associated with the produced event object using the yaml_event_delete() function.

An application must not alternate the calls of yaml_parser_parse() with the calls of yaml_parser_scan() or yaml_parser_load(). Doing this will break the parser.

---

# yaml_parser_scan in unsafe_libyaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unsafe-libyaml/0.2.11/unsafe_libyaml/fn.yaml_parser_scan.html

```
pub unsafe fn yaml_parser_scan(
    parser:
```
[*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html)[yaml_parser_t](https://docs.rs/struct.yaml_parser_t.html),
    token: [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html)[yaml_token_t](https://docs.rs/struct.yaml_token_t.html),
) -> Success## Expand description

Scan the input stream and produce the next token.

Call the function subsequently to produce a sequence of tokens corresponding to the input stream. The initial token has the type YAML_STREAM_START_TOKEN while the ending token has the type YAML_STREAM_END_TOKEN.

An application is responsible for freeing any buffers associated with the produced token object using the yaml_token_delete function.

An application must not alternate the calls of yaml_parser_scan() with the calls of yaml_parser_parse() or yaml_parser_load(). Doing this will break the parser.

---

# yaml_read_handler_t in unsafe_libyaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unsafe-libyaml/0.2.11/unsafe_libyaml/type.yaml_read_handler_t.html

`pub type yaml_read_handler_t = unsafe `[fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.fn.html)(data: [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html)[c_void](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ffi/enum.c_void.html), buffer: [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html)[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html), size: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html), size_read: [*mut ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.pointer.html)[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)) -> [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.i32.html);## Expand description

The prototype of a read handler.

The read handler is called when the parser needs to read more bytes from the
source. The handler should write not more than `size` bytes to the `buffer`.
The number of written bytes should be set to the `length` variable.

On success, the handler should return 1. If the handler failed, the returned
value should be 0. On EOF, the handler should set the `size_read` to 0 and
return 1.

---

# yaml_write_handler_t in unsafe_libyaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unsafe-libyaml/0.2.11/unsafe_libyaml/type.yaml_write_handler_t.html

## Expand description

The prototype of a write handler.

The write handler is called when the emitter needs to flush the accumulated
characters to the output. The handler should write `size` bytes of the
`buffer` to the output.

On success, the handler should return 1. If the handler failed, the returned value should be 0.

---

- Set if unescaped non-ASCII characters are allowed.

- Set the preferred line width. -1 means unlimited.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_event_delete.html)- event_ - delete - ⚠
- Free any memory allocated for an event object.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_mapping_end_event_initialize.html)- mapping_ - end_ - event_ - initialize - ⚠
- Create a MAPPING-END event.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_mapping_start_event_initialize.html)- mapping_ - start_ - event_ - initialize - ⚠
- Create a MAPPING-START event.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_parser_delete.html)- parser_ - delete - ⚠
- Destroy a parser.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_parser_initialize.html)- parser_ - initialize - ⚠
- Initialize a parser.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_parser_load.html)- parser_ - load - ⚠
- Parse the input stream and produce the next YAML document.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_parser_parse.html)- parser_ - parse - ⚠
- Parse the input stream and produce the next parsing event.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_parser_scan.html)- parser_ - scan - ⚠
- Scan the input stream and produce the next token.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_parser_set_encoding.html)- parser_ - set_ - encoding - ⚠
- Set the source encoding.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_parser_set_input.html)- parser_ - set_ - input - ⚠
- Set a generic input handler.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_parser_set_input_string.html)- parser_ - set_ - input_ - string - ⚠
- Set a string input.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_scalar_event_initialize.html)- scalar_ - event_ - initialize - ⚠
- Create a SCALAR event.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_sequence_end_event_initialize.html)- sequence_ - end_ - event_ - initialize - ⚠
- Create a SEQUENCE-END event.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_sequence_start_event_initialize.html)- sequence_ - start_ - event_ - initialize - ⚠
- Create a SEQUENCE-START event.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_stream_end_event_initialize.html)- stream_ - end_ - event_ - initialize - ⚠
- Create the STREAM-END event.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_stream_start_event_initialize.html)- stream_ - start_ - event_ - initialize - ⚠
- Create the STREAM-START event.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/fn.yaml_token_delete.html)- token_ - delete - ⚠
- Free any memory allocated for a token object.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/type.yaml_node_item_t.html)- node_ - item_ - t
- An element of a sequence node.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/type.yaml_read_handler_t.html)- read_ - handler_ - t
- The prototype of a read handler.
- [yaml_](https://docs.rs/type.yaml_write_handler_t.html)- write_ - handler_ - t
- The prototype of a write handler.

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# pretty_assertions 1.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty_assertions/^1.0

# Pretty Assertions

Overwrite `assert_eq!` with a drop-in replacement, adding a colorful diff.

## Usage

When writing tests in Rust, you'll probably use `assert_eq!(a, b)` *a lot*.

If such a test fails, it will present all the details of `a` and `b`.
But you have to spot the differences yourself, which is not always straightforward,
like here:

Wouldn't that task be *much* easier with a colorful diff?

Yep — and you only need **one line of code** to make it happen:

```
use ;
```
```
// 1. add the `pretty_assertions` dependency to `Cargo.toml`.
// 2. insert this line at the top of each module, as needed
use ;
```
## Semantic Versioning

The exact output of assertions is **not guaranteed** to be consistent over time, and may change between minor versions.
The output of this crate is designed to be read by a human. It is not suitable for exact comparison, for example in snapshot testing.

This crate adheres to semantic versioning for publically exported crate items, **except** the `private` module, which may change between any version.

## Tip

Specify it as [ [dev-dependencies]](http://doc.crates.io/specifying-dependencies.html#development-dependencies)
and it will only be used for compiling tests, examples, and benchmarks.
This way the compile time of

`cargo build` won't be affected!Also add `#[cfg(test)]` to your `use` statements, like this:

```
use ;
```
## Notes

- Since `Rust 2018`edition, you need to declare`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`per module. Before you would write`#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions;`.
- The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries you include.
- `assert_ne`is also switched to multi-line presentation, but does- *not*show a diff.
- Under Windows, the terminal state is modified to properly handle VT100 escape sequences, which may break display for certain use cases.
- The minimum supported rust version (MSRV) is 1.35.0

`no_std` support

For `no_std` support, disable the `std` feature and enable the `alloc` feature:

```
# Cargo.toml
 = { = "...",  = false,  = ["alloc"] }
```

at your option.

# yansi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yansi/^1.0.1/

## Expand description

A dead simple ANSI terminal color painting library.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Why *y*et another *ANSI* terminal coloring library? Here are some reasons:

- This library makes simple things *simple*:`use``Paint`
- Zero dependencies by default. It really is simple.
- Zero allocations except as needed by opt-in [wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping).
- [Automatic Windows support](https://docs.rs#windows)for the vast majority (95%+) of Windows users.
- [Featureful](https://docs.rs#crate-features), no-- `no_std`- `alloc`, support with- `default-features = false`.
- `Style`constructors are- `const`
- *Any*type implementing a formatting trait can be styled, not just strings.
- Styling can be [enabled](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html)and[disabled](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)globally and[dynamically](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html), on the fly.
- A `Style`can be predicated on arbitrary[conditions](https://docs.rs#per-style).
- Formatting specifiers like `{:x}`and`{:08b}`are supported and preserved!
- [Built-in (optional) conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions)for- [TTY detection](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-1)and- [common environment variables](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#impl-Condition-2).
- Arbitrary items can be *masked*
- Styling can *wrap*
- Styling can *linger*
- Experimental support for [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)is included.
- The name `yansi`is pretty cool 😎.

All that said, `yansi` borrows API ideas from older libraries as well as
implementation details from [ ansi_term](https://crates.io/crates/ansi_term).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The [ Paint](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html) trait is implemented for every type. Import it and call
chainable builder methods:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Testing, {}, {}, {}!",
    "Ready".bold(),
    "Set".yellow().italic(),
    "STOP".white().on_red().bright().underline().bold());
```
`>` Testing,
**Ready**,
* Set*,

__!__

**STOP**The methods return a [ Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html) type which consists of a

[and a reference to the receiver. Displaying a](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style`[(via](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``print!()`,
`format!()`, etc) results in emitting ANSI escape codes that effectuate the
style.[§](https://docs.rs#uniform-const-builders)Uniform `const` Builders

All builder methods are uniformly available for [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)

`Color`[, which means you can chain calls across library types. All methods are](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``const`, allowing creations of `const` or `static` [s. A](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)

`Style``Style` can be directly applied to values with [, from](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#method.paint)

`.paint()`[, available for every type:](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#method.paint)

`Paint::paint()````
use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*};
// `const` constructors allow static `Style`s for easy reuse
static ALERT: Style = White.bright().underline().italic().on_red();
println!("Testing, {}, {}, {}!",
    "Ready".bold(),
    "Set".yellow().bold(),
    "STOP".paint(ALERT));
```
`>` Testing,
**Ready**,
**Set**,
__ STOP__!

[§](https://docs.rs#conditional-styling)Conditional Styling

[§](https://docs.rs#globally)Globally

Styling is enabled by default but can be enabled and disabled globally via
[ enable()](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html) and

[. When styling is disabled, no ANSI escape codes are emitted, and](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)

`disable()`[values are omitted entirely.](https://docs.rs#masking)

*masked*Global styling can also be dynamically enabled and disabled using
[ whenever()](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html) with an arbitrary

[: a function that returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html)

`Condition``true` or `false`. This condition is evaluated each time a [item is displayed. The associated styling is enabled, and mask values emitted, exactly when and only when the condition returns](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)

`Painted``true`.[§](https://docs.rs#per-style)Per-`Style`

A specific `Style` can itself be conditionally applied by using
[ .whenever()](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html#method.whenever):

```
use yansi::{Paint, Style, Color::*, Condition};
static WARNING: Style = Black.bold().on_yellow().whenever(Condition::STDERR_IS_TTY);
eprintln!("{}", "Bees can sting!".paint(WARNING));
```
With the above, if `stderr` is a TTY, then:
`>` **Bees can sting!**

If it is not a TTY, styling is not emitted:
`>` Bees can sting!

See [ Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html) for a list of built-in conditions which require enabling
crate features.

[§](https://docs.rs#quirks)Quirks

As a convenience, `yansi` implements several “quirks”, applicable via
[ Quirk](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html) and the respective methods, that modify if and how styling is
presented to the terminal. These quirks do not correspond to any ANSI
styling sequences.

[§](https://docs.rs#masking)Masking

Items can be arbitrarily *masked* with the [ mask()](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html#tymethod.mask) builder
method. Masked values are not emitted when styling is disabled, globally or
for a given style. This allows selective output based on whether styling is
enabled.

One use for this feature is to print certain characters only when styling is enabled. For instance, you might wish to emit the 🎨 emoji when coloring is enabled but not otherwise. This can be accomplished by masking the emoji:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("I like colors!{}", " 🎨".mask());
```
When styling is enabled, this prints: `>` I like colors! 🎨

With styling disabled, this prints: `>` I like colors!

[§](https://docs.rs#wrapping)Wrapping

**Note:** *Either the  std or alloc feature is required for wrapping.
std is enabled by default. See *

[crate features](https://docs.rs#crate-features).

Styling can *wrap* via [ Quirk::Wrap](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Wrap) or the equivalent

[constructor. A wrapping style modifies any styling resets emitted by the internal value so that they correspond to the wrapping style. In other words, the “reset” style of the wrapped item is modified to be the style being](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.wrap)

`wrap()``.wrap()`d.Wrapping is useful in situations where opaque and arbitrary values must be styled consistently irrespective of any existing styling. For example, a generic logger might want to style messages based on log levels consistently, even when those messages may already include styling. Wrapping exists to enable such consistent styling:

```
use yansi::Paint;
// Imagine that `inner` is opaque and we don't know it's styling.
let inner = format!("{} and {}", "Stop".red(), "Go".green());
// We can use `wrap` to ensure anything in `inner` not styled is blue.
println!("Hey! {}", inner.blue().wrap());
```
Thanks to wrapping, this prints:
`>` Hey!
Stop and
Go

Without wrapping, the reset after `"Stop".red()` would not be overwritten:
`>` Hey! Stop and Go

Wrapping incurs a performance cost due to an extra allocation and replacement if the wrapped item has styling applied to it. Otherwise, it does not allocate nor incur a meaningful performance cost.

[§](https://docs.rs#lingering)Lingering

Styling can *linger* beyond a single value via [ Quirk::Linger](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Linger) or the
equivalent

[constructor. A lingering style does not reset itself after being applied. In other words, the style lingers on beyond the value it’s applied to, until something else resets the respective styling.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.linger)

`linger()`The complement to lingering is force resetting via [ Quirk::Resetting](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Resetting) or
the equivalent

[constructor. Force resetting, as the name implies, forces a reset suffix to be emitted after the value, irrespective of any lingering applied. It can be used as a way to finalize a lingering style.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.resetting)

`resetting()`Lingering itself is useful in situations where a given style is to be
repeated across multiple values, or when style is intended to persist even
across values that are not styled with `yansi`. It also allows avoiding
unnecessarily repeated ANSI code sequences. The examples below illustrate
some scenarios in which lingering is useful:

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic().linger(),
    "you".on_yellow(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "today".blue());
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are things with you__
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("Hello! {} {} things with {} {}?",
    "How".magenta().underline().linger(),
    "are".italic(), // doesn't linger, so all styling is reset here
    "you".on_yellow().linger(),
    "today".blue()); // doesn't linger; styling is reset
```
`>` Hello!
__How  are__
things with
you
today?

```
use yansi::Paint;
println!("{} B {} {} {} F",
    "A".red().linger(),
    "C".underline().linger(),
    "D", // doesn't linger, but no styling applied, thus no reset
    "E".resetting());  // explicitly reset
```
`>`  A B __C D E__  F

[§](https://docs.rs#brightening)Brightening

Most pimrary colors are available in regular and *bright* variants, e.g.,
[ Color::Red](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.Red) and

[. The](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html#variant.BrightRed)

`Color::BrightRed`[and](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.Bright)

`Quirk::Bright`[quirks, typically applied via](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html#variant.OnBright)

`Quirk::OnBright`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.bright)

`.bright()`[, provide an alternative, convenient mechanism to select the bright variant of the selected foreground or background color, respectively. The quirk provides no additional colors and is equivalent to selecting the bright variants directly.](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html#method.on_bright)

`.on_bright()````
use yansi::Paint;
// These are all equivalent.
print!("{}", "Regular".red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright_red());
print!("{}", "Bright".bright().red());
print!("{}", "Bright".red().bright());
// The `bright` quirk lets use choose the bright variants of _any_ color,
// even when the color or style is unknown at the call site.
print!("{}", "Normal".paint(STYLE));
print!("{}", "Bright".paint(STYLE).bright());
```
`>` Regular
Bright
Bright
Bright
**Normal**
**Bright**

The `bright()` quirk can be applied before or after a color is selected
while having the same effect.

[§](https://docs.rs#windows)Windows

Styling is supported and enabled automatically on Windows beginning with
the Windows 10 Anniversary Update, or about [96% of all Windows machines
worldwide](https://gs.statcounter.com/os-version-market-share/windows/desktop/worldwide),
and likely closer to 100% of developer machines (e.g., 99% of visitors to
[rocket.rs](https://rocket.rs) on Windows are on Windows 10+).

Yansi enables styling support on Windows by querying the Windows API on the first attempt to color. If support is available, it is enabled. If support is not available, styling is disabled and no styling sequences are emitted.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

| Feature | Default? | Also Enables | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std` | Y | `alloc` | Use `std`library. |
| `alloc` | Y | Use `alloc`. Enables[wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping). | |
| `detect-tty` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `detect-env` | N | `std` | See [optional conditions](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html#built-in-conditions). |
| `hyperlink` | N | `std` | Enables [hyperlinking](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)support. |

With `default-features = false`, this crate is `#[no_std]`.

Without any features enabled, all functionality except [wrapping](https://docs.rs#wrapping) is
available. To recover wrapping *with* `#[no_std]`, set `default-features = false` and enable the `alloc` feature, which requires `alloc` support.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [hyperlink](https://docs.rs/hyperlink/index.html)- `hyperlink`
- Experimental support for hyperlinking.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Condition](https://docs.rs/struct.Condition.html)
- A function that decides whether styling should be applied.
- [Painted](https://docs.rs/struct.Painted.html)
- An arbitrary value with a `Style`
- [Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)
- A set of styling options.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/enum.Attribute.html)
- Enum representing text attributes, largely for text formatting.
- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.Color.html)
- Enum representing a terminal color.
- [Quirk](https://docs.rs/enum.Quirk.html)
- Enum representing a `yansi`quirk.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Paint](https://docs.rs/trait.Paint.html)
- A trait to apply styling to any value. Implemented for all types.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [disable](https://docs.rs/fn.disable.html)
- Unconditionally disables styling globally.
- [enable](https://docs.rs/fn.enable.html)
- Unconditionally enables styling globally.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_enabled.html)- enabled
- Returns `true`if styling is globally enabled and`false`otherwise.
- [whenever](https://docs.rs/fn.whenever.html)
- Dynamically enables and disables styling globally based on `condition`.
